prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: American Time Use Survey (ATUS)
Description: The American Time Use Survey (ATUS) provides nationally representative estimates of how, where, and with whom Americans spend their time, and is the only federal survey providing data on the full range of nonmarket activities. These activities include work, childcare, housework, watching television, volunteering, and socializing.
URL: https://www.bls.gov/tus

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Mark any field not directly observable as unknown rather than inferring it.

American Time Use Survey News Release

For release 10:00 a.m. (ET) Thursday, June 25, 2026	                                   USDL-26-1022

 Technical information:       (202) 691-6339  *  atusinfo@bls.gov  *  www.bls.gov/tus
 Media contact:               (202) 691-5902  *  PressOffice@bls.gov


                           AMERICAN TIME USE SURVEY - 2025 RESULTS


In 2025, 35 percent of employed people did some or all of their work at home on days they worked,
and 70 percent of employed people did some or all of their work at their workplace, the U.S. 
Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. 

These and other results from the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) were released today. They include
the average amount of time per day in 2025 that individuals worked, did household activities, and
engaged in leisure and sports activities. Additionally, measures of the average time per day spent
providing childcare--both as a primary (or main) activity and while doing other things are provided.
For a detailed description of ATUS data and methodology, see the Technical Note.

Working (by Employed People) in 2025

 --On days they worked, full-time employed people worked an average of 8.1 hours. They worked 8.5
   hours on an average weekday and 5.5 hours on an average weekend day. (See table 4.)

 --Many more people worked on weekdays than on weekend days: 81 percent of employed people worked
   on an average weekday, compared with 30 percent on an average weekend day. (See table 4.)

 --Among those who worked on an average weekend day, those with lower levels of education worked
   more hours than those with a bachelor's degree or higher. On weekend days they worked, high
   school graduates with no college spent 6.4 hours working, compared with 4.0 hours for those with 
   a bachelor's degree or higher. (See table 4.)

 --On days they worked, 35 percent of employed people did some or all of their work at home and 70
   percent of employed people did some or all of their work at their workplace. Employed women (38
   percent) were more likely to work at home than employed men (31 percent). (See table 6.)

 --Among workers age 25 and over, those with higher levels of education were more likely to work at
   home than were those who had less education. Fifty-one percent of employed people with a 
   bachelor's degree or higher performed some work at home on days worked, compared with 19 percent
   of those with a high school diploma and no college. Workers with a bachelor's degree or higher
   were also more likely to work on an average day than were those with a high school diploma and
   no college--72 percent, compared with 63 percent. (See table 6.)

Household Activities in 2025

 --On an average day, 81 percent of people engaged in household activities--such as housework,
   cooking, lawn care, or household management--spending about 2 hours on these activities.
   (See table 1.)

 --Eighty-seven percent of women and 75 percent of men spent some time doing household activities
   on an average day. On the days they did household activities, women spent an average of 2.8
   hours on these activities, while men spent 2.1 hours doing so. (See table 1.)

 --Time spent doing household activities increased with age. On an average day, individuals ages 15
   to 19 spent 43 minutes engaged in household activities, while those age 65 and over spent 2.7
   hours doing so. (See table 3.) 

 --Among adults living with children under age 18, those who were not employed spent over an hour
   more than those who were employed doing household activities on an average day--3.1 hours
   compared to 1.7 hours. (See tables 8B and 8C.) 

 --More people engaged in housework on weekend days than on weekdays, on average--40 percent,
   compared with 35 percent. However, people were slightly more likely to do food preparation and
   cleanup on weekdays than weekend days--66 percent, compared to 63 percent. (See table 2.)

Leisure and Sports Activities in 2025

 --Nearly everyone age 15 and over (95 percent) engaged in some sort of leisure and sport activity,
   such as watching TV, socializing, or exercising on an average day. Men were slightly more likely
   to engage in leisure and sports activities than women (96 percent compared with 94 percent) and
   also spent more time in these activities than did women (5.6 hours, compared with 4.8 hours).
   (See table 1.)

 --On average, adults age 75 and over spent 7.4 hours engaged in leisure and sports activities per
   day--more than any other age group. Those ages 35 to 44 averaged 3.9 hours doing leisure and
   sports activities per day--less than all other age groups. (See table 11A.) 

 --Watching TV was the leisure and sports activity that occupied the most time (2.6 hours per day),
   accounting for half of all leisure time, on average (5.2 hours). (See table 1 and table 11A.) 

 --People were less likely to engage in socializing and communicating on an average day in 2025
   than in 2015--30 percent compared with 38 percent. They also spent less time in these activities
   in 2025 than in 2015--35 minutes compared with 41 minutes. (See tables 1 and 11A.)

 --Individuals spent more time playing games or using a computer on an average day in 2025 than
   they did in 2015 (37 minutes compared with 25 minutes). This includes time spent playing board
   games, video games, using social media, and other computer activities done for leisure.
   Individuals ages 15 to 19 spent 1.5 hours playing games or using a computer for leisure on an
   average day in 2025, more than any other age group. (See table 11A.)

 --Employed adults living in households with no children under age 18 engaged in leisure and sports
   activities for 4.5 hours per day, over an hour more than did employed adults living with a child
   under age 6 (3.2 hours). (See table 8B.)

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: American Time Use Survey (ATUS)
Description: The American Time Use Survey (ATUS) provides nationally representative estimates of how, where, and with whom Americans spend their time, and is the only federal survey providing data on the full range of nonmarket activities. These activities include work, childcare, housework, watching television, volunteering, and socializing.
URL: https://www.bls.gov/tus

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# American Time Use Survey (ATUS): Dataset Report

**Bottom line:** Your title, description and URL are accurate. The description closely follows BLS's own wording. But the survey is getting weaker: response rates have fallen from 57.8% in 2003 to 25.7% in 2025, and completed interviews from about 20,700 to about 6,100. The 2025 data also has a six-week gap because of the government shutdown. The survey has no statutory mandate of its own, which matters because BLS's FY2026 and FY2027 budgets say it will focus on programs that are major economic indicators or required by statute.

My searches hit a limit partway through. Items marked **[unverified]** come from my background knowledge and should be checked against the BLS documents linked below.

---

## 1. Checking your information

| Element | Your version | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Title | American Time Use Survey (ATUS) | Correct |
| Description | "...only federal survey providing data on the full range of nonmarket activities..." | Accurate. It matches BLS's budget justification wording almost word for word: "the only federal survey that provides data on the full range of nonmarket activities, from childcare to volunteering." |
| URL | https://www.bls.gov/tus | Works. The official address ends in a slash: `https://www.bls.gov/tus/` |

**Small corrections:**
- "Americans" means the civilian, non-institutionalized population **age 15 and over**. Children under 15 and people in institutions (prisons, nursing homes) are not covered.
- The estimates describe an **average day**, overall and separately for weekdays and weekends. They do not follow any one person's whole week.
- "With whom" and "where" are recorded for most activities, but not all of them (sleeping and grooming, for example, are excluded).

---

## 2. Who publishes it

- **Sponsor and publisher:** U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Department of Labor. It sits in the Labor Force Statistics / Employment and Unemployment Statistics budget area.
- **Data collector:** U.S. Census Bureau, by telephone from its call center under an agreement with BLS.
- **Contact:** atusinfo@bls.gov, (202) 691-6339
- **Module sponsors (past and present):** DOL Women's Bureau (Leave and Job Flexibilities modules). The Eating and Health module is sponsored by USDA's Economic Research Service, and the Well-Being module had National Institute on Aging support **[sponsors unverified]**. Under BLS policy, any federal agency, 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(1) organization, or a group including one of these can sponsor a module. The sponsor pays all BLS and Census costs, and modules run for at least one calendar year.

---

## 3. Legal authority and mandate

**General authority, not a specific mandate.** No law requires the ATUS by name.
- **BLS's founding law (1884), 29 U.S.C. 1:** the Bureau is to gather information on labor "in the most general and comprehensive sense," including "the hours of labor" and "social, intellectual, and moral prosperity." The FY2027 budget justification quotes this.
- **29 U.S.C. 2:** BLS's authority to make agreements such as the one with Census.
- **Title 13 U.S.C.:** Census confidentiality rules apply. BLS's module policy says only data that comply with Title 13 will be released.
- **CIPSEA (Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act), reauthorized in the 2018 Evidence Act:** confidentiality and statistical-use-only protections **[applies to BLS generally]**.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act:** OMB must approve the survey. The core ATUS clearance is OMB 1220-0175 **[core number inferred from a Federal Register notice]**. The Leave module is 1220-0191.
- **Participation is voluntary [unverified].**
- **OMB Statistical Policy Directive No. 4** governs how the data are released.

**International inspiration (not binding):** the 1995 UN Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing. Its Platform for Action (item 206) called on national statistics offices to "conduct regular time-use studies to measure, in quantitative terms, unremunerated work."

**Why this matters for advocates:**
- The FY2026 and FY2027 budget requests both say BLS will focus on programs that are "Principal Federal Economic Indicators (PFEIs), required by statute, or in use in current law."
- The FY2026 Department of Labor plan mentions "consideration of more significant targeted changes to or eliminations of survey programs."
- The ATUS is not statutory and, as far as I know, not a PFEI **[check against OMB's PFEI list]**.

---

## 4. History

| Date | Milestone |
|---|---|
| Oct 24, 1991 | Rep. Barbara-Rose Collins introduces the Unremunerated Work Act (it died in committee). BLS sets up a time-use working group. |
| 1995 | UN Beijing conference; the BLS Commissioner reconvenes the working group to study feasibility. |
| 1997 | BLS hires Westat for a telephone pilot study. |
| Nov 20–21, 1997 | BLS and the MacArthur Network on Family and the Economy host the conference "Time Use, Non-market Work, and Family Well-being." |
| 1998 | Working-group plan becomes the survey's blueprint. |
| 1999 | First budget request to OMB; a National Academy of Sciences workshop endorses the BLS design. |
| Dec 2000 | Survey approved and funded. Planned start of Jan 2002 slips to 2003 because of budget delays and new computer systems. |
| 2001–2002 | Field tests by BLS and Census. |
| Jan 2003 | Full data collection begins; 20,720 interviews that year. |
| Dec 2003 / 2004 | Monthly sample cut by 35%; 13,973 interviews in 2004. |
| Sep 14, 2004 | First annual news release. |
| 2005–2010 | Questions on trips added. |
| 2006–08, 2014–16, 2022–23 | Eating and Health module. |
| 2010, 2012–13, Mar–Dec 2021 | Well-Being module. |
| 2011 | Eldercare questions become a permanent part of the survey; first Leave module. |
| 2017–18 | Leave and Job Flexibilities module (about 10,000 respondents). |
| Oct 2016 | ATUS time series added to the BLS online database. |
| Mar 19 – May 10, 2020 | Collection suspended for COVID-19. Normal 2020 annual, Q1 and Q2 estimates could not be published. |
| 2024 | Leave and Job Flexibilities module approved by OMB (Dec 2023, about $400,000 per year in federal cost, clearance expires 12/31/2026). The FY2025 budget said BLS would finish fielding it, contingent on sponsor funding. **I could not confirm whether its results have been published.** |
| Oct 1 – Nov 12, 2025 | All ATUS work stopped during the federal shutdown. There are **no diaries for Sept 30 – Nov 11, 2025**. |
| Jun 25, 2026 | 2025 results released (USDL-26-1022). |

---

## 5. Methodology

- **Who is sampled:** households finishing their 8th and final month in the Current Population Survey (CPS), the monthly labor force survey. One person age 15+ is randomly chosen per household. Because of this link, each record carries detailed CPS information on demographics, work status and earnings.
- **Diary day:** each person is assigned a day to report on. 10% are assigned to each weekday and 25% to each weekend day, so weekends are oversampled. The person is called the next day and asked about "yesterday." Calls are repeated on the same weekday for up to 8 weeks.
- **Interview:** computer-assisted telephone interview. It covers activities in sequence from 4 a.m. yesterday to 4 a.m. today, plus where and with whom. It then asks about childcare done alongside other activities ("secondary childcare," for children under 13), eldercare, and work and labor force updates.
- **Coding:** activities are coded with a three-tier, six-digit system: 17 major categories at the top level. The coding lexicons are specific to each year, so check them when comparing years.
- **Weights:** they adjust for the sample design and for nonresponse, including missing days. For each quarter, the weights add up to the population times the number of days. Replicate weights are provided for standard errors (160 successive-difference replicates **[unverified]**).
- **Response-rate formula:** AAPOR Response Rate 2. Published rates are calculated before final editing; dropping poor-quality cases (fewer than 5 activities, or 3+ hours refused or "don't remember") lowers them by 1–3 points.

**Response rates (%)**

| Year | Rate |
|---|---|
| 2003 | 57.8 |
| 2007 | 52.5 |
| 2010 | 56.9 |
| 2013 | 49.9 |
| 2016 | 46.8 |
| 2019 | 42.0 |
| 2020 | 39.2 |
| 2022 | 35.8 |
| 2023 | 36.9 |
| 2024 | 32.4 |
| **2025** | **25.7** |

- A 2004 study found the main reason people refuse is fatigue from having already done eight months of the CPS.
- Sample size is shrinking: BLS's budget documents describe about 650 interviews a month in FY2026 and about 600 a month in FY2027. Actual completes in 2025 were about 6,100.

---

## 6. Data products and formats

1. **Annual news release** (late June) with tables, plus a Technical Note.
2. **Online database and API:** time series under the "TU" prefix. Bulk files are probably at `download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/tu/` **[path unverified]**.
3. **Public-use microdata** (bls.gov/tus/data.htm): single-year and multi-year (2003–present) files.
   - Files: Respondent, Roster, Activity, Activity Summary, Who, ATUS–CPS, Eldercare Roster, Replicate Weights.
   - Delimited .dat files with SAS, Stata and SPSS setup code **[file list from background knowledge]**.
   - Separate module files.
4. **Documentation:** User's Guide; the "Changes Between the 2003–2025 Data Files" document; data dictionaries; coding lexicons; questionnaires; Handbook of Methods chapter (bls.gov/opub/hom/atus/); module policy; shutdown and COVID notices.
5. **Interactive charts**, plus articles in the Monthly Labor Review, TED (The Economics Daily) and Beyond the Numbers.
6. **Restricted data** through BLS's restricted-access program.

**Third-party access:**
- **IPUMS ATUS (ATUS-X)**, atusdata.org, run by the University of Minnesota and the University of Maryland. It is free with registration, harmonizes years, and lets users build custom time-use variables. Citation DOI: 10.18128/D060.
- Related IPUMS collections: AHTUS (U.S. time diaries, 1930–present) and MTUS (multi-country, with University College London's time-use centre).

---

## 7. Notes for preservationists and data librarians

- **Copies elsewhere:**
  - The St. Louis Fed's FRASER archive holds ATUS news releases as PDFs (e.g., the 2024 release).
  - IPUMS says its goals include "to collect and preserve ATUS data and documentation" and keeps versioned, fixed-format archived copies.
  - ICPSR and Data.gov may also hold copies **[unverified]**.
- **Priority items to capture:**
  - Every year's microdata and the multi-year files.
  - Year-specific coding lexicons and data dictionaries.
  - User's Guide, changes document, questionnaires and interviewer materials.
  - Replicate weights and all module files (EH, WB, Leave, 2024 Leave if released).
  - The time-series flat files.
  - Notices on the 2020 COVID suspension and the 2025 shutdown.
  - Archived news releases from 2004 on.
- **Versioning:** BLS sometimes reissues files and changes variables. The changes document records sample cuts, collection breaks, questionnaire changes and weighting changes. Keep each version with its date.
- **Rights:** BLS products are U.S. government works in the public domain. Ask users to cite BLS and, if used, IPUMS.
- **Known gaps:**
  - Mar 19 – May 10, 2020 (COVID).
  - Sept 30 – Nov 11, 2025 (shutdown). BLS says the effect on estimates "is not possible to quantify."

---

## 8. Notes for data scientists

- **Always use the weights.** Unweighted results are biased because weekends are oversampled and nonresponse is uneven.
- **Small samples:** pool several years for subgroups. State-level estimates generally aren't reliable.
- **Linking:** IDs match to CPS records, which allows extra variables and research on nonresponse.
- **Limits of the design:**
  - One day per person, so no week-to-week variation for an individual.
  - Recall error.
  - Telephone only.
  - Most simultaneous activities are not coded, except childcare, eldercare and (via IPUMS) eating and drinking.
  - Possible nonresponse bias, especially now that response is around 26% (busy people may be less likely to answer).
- **Breaks in the series to account for:** 2003 vs. later years (sample size), 2020 (COVID), late 2025 (missing data), and coding-lexicon revisions.
- **Recent findings (2025):**
  - 35% of employed people did some work at home on days they worked.
  - Full-time workers averaged 8.1 hours on days worked.
  - TV took 2.6 of 5.2 daily leisure hours.
  - Socializing fell from 38% of people on an average day in 2015 to 30% in 2025 (41 to 35 minutes).
  - Gaming and leisure computer use rose from 25 to 37 minutes.
  - Women did household activities 2.8 hours on days they did them; men 2.1 hours.

---

## 9. Typical users

- **Federal:**
  - BEA, for alternative GDP measures that value unpaid household work (likely its household production satellite account **[name unverified]**).
  - BLS Employment Projections.
  - The Federal Interagency Forums on Aging-Related Statistics and on Child and Family Statistics.
  - DOL Women's Bureau, USDA ERS and NIH-funded researchers.
- **International:** OECD and the UN, for comparing countries.
- **Academic:** economists, sociologists, demographers, public health researchers (sleep, physical activity, eating), and transportation and gender researchers.
- **Legal and forensic economists:** valuing lost household services in injury and wrongful-death cases **[common practice; not checked in this session]**.
- **Energy and building modelers:** occupancy schedules (e.g., NREL's ResStock **[unverified]**).
- **Advocates and journalists:** caregiving, paid leave, gender equity, loneliness, screen time and remote work.

---

## 10. Public benefits

- **Makes unpaid work visible:** childcare, eldercare and housework, as the Beijing Platform called for.
- **Feeds policy debates:** childcare, caregiving support, paid leave and flexible schedules (Leave module), the gender gap in unpaid work, and telework.
- **Provides health and well-being measures:** sleep, exercise, eating, social isolation.
- **Supports fuller national accounting:** measures of economic activity beyond market GDP.
- **Free public data** with documentation dating back to 2003.

---

## 11. Risks and issues for advocates

1. **Response rates have collapsed** (57.8% to 25.7%), raising questions about bias and reliability.
2. **The sample keeps shrinking:** about 20,700 interviews in 2003, about 6,100 in 2025, and about 600 a month planned for FY2027.
3. **Budget and staffing pressure:**
   - BLS funding: $703.95M in FY2025, $708.5M in FY2026, and $667.95M requested for FY2027.
   - Staff (full-time equivalents): 2,019 in FY2025 down to 1,773 in FY2026.
   - The FY2026 and FY2027 budgets propose moving BLS into the Commerce Department alongside Census and BEA.
   - BLS says it will prioritize indicator and statutory programs, and the ATUS is neither.
4. **Modules depend on sponsors paying.** Whether the 2024 Leave module was completed and released is unclear.
5. **Collection is fragile:** shutdowns and emergencies have created permanent holes in the data.
6. **Possible actions:**
   - Push for a statutory basis or PFEI-like protection.
   - Fund modules or advocate for them.
   - Comment on Federal Register PRA notices.
   - Support archiving through IPUMS and FRASER.

---

## Key sources
- ATUS home: https://www.bls.gov/tus/
- 2025 results: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/atus_06252026.htm
- 2024 results: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/atus_06262025.htm
- Handbook of Methods, history: https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/atus/history.htm
- User's Guide (response rates): https://www.bls.gov/tus/atususersguide.pdf
- Changes between data files: https://www.bls.gov/tus/other-documentation/changes.pdf
- 2025 shutdown notice: https://www.bls.gov/tus/notices/2026/october2025shutdown.htm
- Modules: https://www.bls.gov/tus/modules/modules.htm
- Module policy: https://www.bls.gov/tus/modules/modulepolicy.pdf
- MLR 2004, "Planning, designing, and executing the BLS ATUS": https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2004/10/art1full.pdf
- BLS budget justifications, FY2026 and FY2027 (dol.gov)
- 2024 Leave module clearance (OMB 1220-0191): reginfo.gov
- IPUMS ATUS: https://www.atusdata.org
- FRASER release archive: fraser.stlouisfed.org

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

# American Time Use Survey (ATUS): Risk Assessment

ATUS is still being collected and published. The 2025 results came out on schedule, and its OMB approval to collect data runs through September 2028. The risks are a smaller, less precise survey and pressure on BLS, not deletion. Two of six categories are No Known Issue or Moderate each, and three are High: data quality, statutory context, and staffing and funding.

**Correction to my earlier report:** I wasn't sure whether the 2024 Leave and Job Flexibilities module had been published. It has. BLS released "Access to and Use of Leave" tables comparing 2017–18 with 2024–25, last updated August 26, 2026 ([BLS leave table 1](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/leave.t01.htm)).

**Staffing tracker:** The usajobs-tracker page loaded, but the BLS figures load by script and didn't come through. The site also says it stopped updating on Dec 31, 2025. Staffing figures below come from budget documents and press reports instead.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue**

**Evidence for No Known Issue**
- Microdata files and documentation for 2003–2025 are still on bls.gov/tus/data.htm (page dated June 25, 2026).
- The "Changes Between the 2003–2025 Data Files" document is still posted. It records method changes openly instead of removing anything.
- Copies exist outside BLS: IPUMS ATUS (atusdata.org) and the St. Louis Fed's FRASER archive of news releases.

**Evidence for Moderate or High Risk**
- I found no files or variables removed after release.
- The 2020 COVID gap (Mar 19 – May 10) and the 2025 shutdown gap (Sept 30 – Nov 11) are periods that were never collected, not data taken down. They are disclosed in BLS notices ([shutdown notice](https://www.bls.gov/tus/notices/2026/october2025shutdown.htm)).

**Rationale:** Past data is intact, and good copies exist elsewhere.

## 2. Future Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence for No Known Issue**
- The 2025 annual results came out June 25, 2026, on the usual late-June schedule.
- OMB approval number 1220-0175 was extended without change on Sept 29, 2025, a day before it would have expired. A further minor change was approved Jan 12, 2026, and approval now runs to **09/30/2028** ([reginfo ICR](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202512-1220-003); [Federal Register, June 26, 2025](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/06/26/2025-11766/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-for-omb-review-american-time-use-survey)).
- The FY2027 budget justification still describes ATUS as an ongoing program, at about 600 interviews a month.

**Evidence for Moderate or High Risk**
- During the Oct 1 – Nov 12, 2025 shutdown, all ATUS work stopped. No diary days from Sept 30 – Nov 11, 2025 were collected, which counts as collection skipped for part of a year.
- BLS says it is "not possible to quantify" how the gap affects the 2025 estimates.

**Rationale:** The annual release was on time and approval is current. But the six-week gap is a real interruption to collection, which is Moderate rather than High. It wasn't a full skipped year, and no statutory deadline was missed.

## 3. Data Quality: **High Risk**

**Evidence for High Risk**
- **Fewer published estimates:** BLS's performance target for ATUS annual estimates drops from 11,100–11,877 to **9,300** in FY2027 ([FY2027 BLS budget justification](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/general/budget/2027/CBJ-2027-V3-01.pdf)).
- **Smaller sample:** about 650 interviews a month in FY2026 and about 600 in FY2027. Completed interviews were about 6,100 in 2025, compared with 20,720 in 2003.
- **Response rates falling fast:** 32.4% in 2024 and 25.7% in 2025. OMB approval documents say respondent numbers fell "due to lower response rates."
- **Missing period:** the six-week shutdown gap in 2025.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk**
- The methods are unchanged, and BLS describes ongoing work to raise response rates.
- The 2025 release and the 2024–25 Leave module still came out on schedule.

**Rationale:** The planned 16–22% cut in published estimates is a direct loss of detail, which meets the High threshold.

## 4. Statutory Context: **High Risk**

**Evidence for High Risk**
- No law requires ATUS by name. It relies only on BLS's broad 1884 founding law, 29 U.S.C. 1 ("hours of labor... social, intellectual, and moral prosperity").
- It doesn't seem to be a Principal Federal Economic Indicator (I didn't check OMB's official list), and no federal program needs it to operate.

**Evidence for Moderate or No Known Issue**
- No other federal survey can substitute. BLS calls ATUS "the only federal survey" covering the full range of unpaid activities.
- Others use it, though none of these uses is required by law: BEA, BLS Employment Projections, two federal interagency statistics forums (aging, and child and family), the OECD and the UN.

**Rationale:** The rubric treats vague authorization alone as High Risk. The lack of any substitute is a strong reason to keep it, but that doesn't change the rating.

## 5. Staffing and Funding: **High Risk**

**Evidence for High Risk**
- **Leadership removed:** President Trump fired Commissioner Erika McEntarfer in August 2025 ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/white-house-defends-firing-labor-official-critics-warn-trust-erosion-2025-08-04/)).
- A third of senior BLS posts were reported vacant in late 2025 ([Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/bls-leadership-vacuum-extends-beyond-head-as-key-roles-sit-empty)).
- The FY2026 request would have zeroed BLS's main funding in the Labor Department budget by moving it to Commerce. Only the $68M from Unemployment Insurance trust funds would have stayed.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk**
- **Staff losses:** about 20% since January 2025, from deferred resignations, firings of probationary employees and a hiring freeze ([NPR, Groshen interview](https://www.npr.org/2025/09/08/nx-s1-5530145/former-head-of-the-bureau-of-labor-statistics-discusses-future-of-u-s-labor-data)). Full-time-equivalent staff went from 2,019 (FY2025) to 1,773 (FY2026), down 12%, and 1,754 are requested for FY2027.
- The FY2027 request makes "recent staffing reductions" permanent.

**Evidence for No Known Issue**
- FY2026 funding as enacted was $708.5M, slightly above FY2025's $703.95M. The FY2027 request is $667.95M, about 5.7% lower.
- Brett Matsumoto was confirmed as commissioner on Aug 7, 2026, by a 51–47 vote ([BLS bio](https://www.bls.gov/bls/senior_staff/matsumoto.htm)).
- ATUS's own cost to the government is about $6M a year (per the OMB approval).

**Rationale:** Removing the commissioner meets the High threshold on its own. Staff losses alone would be Moderate.

## 6. Policy: **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence for High Risk**
- None found. There is no presidential-action-driven approval request, no negative policy note on the ATUS site, and no change to ATUS content tied to administration priorities.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk**
- The FY2026 and FY2027 budgets say BLS will focus on programs that are economic indicators, "required by statute, or in use in current law." ATUS has no protection under the first two.
- The FY2026 Labor Department plan mentions "more significant targeted changes to or eliminations of survey programs."
- The proposed merger of BLS, Census and BEA at Commerce is still pending.
- BLS has already cut other programs (CPI data collection, producer price index series) ([Politico](https://www.politico.com/news/2025/06/11/inflation-data-economy-labor-budget-00399155)).

**Evidence for No Known Issue**
- The approval was renewed in 2025 "without change," and the Leave module was fielded and published.

**Rationale:** The changes are proposed or pending, not carried out, so this is Moderate.

---

## Summary
- **Historical Data Availability:** No Known Issue
- **Future Data Availability:** Moderate Risk
- **Data Quality:** High Risk
- **Statutory Context:** High Risk
- **Staffing and Funding:** High Risk
- **Policy:** Moderate Risk
